title: Sunset with someone

cards: You're at the window, and the sky does something extraordinary. Streaks of pink, a band of gold, the clouds lit from underneath. And almost before you think, you call over your shoulder: come here, quick, look at this.
Why do people do that? Nobody else has to see it for it to be real. But something in a person wants company for beauty.
A sunset seen alone is lovely. Seen with someone, it becomes a memory you both hold.

teach.b: Psychologists have tested this urge. In a 2014 study at Yale, people tasted chocolate while another person, a stranger, sat beside them.
Sometimes the stranger was tasting the same chocolate at the same moment; sometimes the stranger was looking at a book of pictures. The two never spoke.
Yet when they tasted together, people rated good chocolate as more delicious, and bitter chocolate as more unpleasant.
Sharing seemed to turn the volume up. A small study, and chocolate isn't a sunset. But it fits an everyday hunch: experiences can feel bigger when someone is in them with you.
There's an old line for this kind of invitation.

In the Gospel of John, a man named Philip has met Jesus and wants his friend Nathanael to meet him too. Nathanael is skeptical, and asks whether anything good can come out of a small town like Nazareth.
Philip doesn't argue. He says simply: "Come and see." Christians read that scene as the start of Nathanael's discipleship, and it means much more to them than a walk.
But the words have lasted as a model of a certain kind of invitation: no persuading, no explaining, just come, and see for yourself.
That's the invitation tonight. Not a speech about sunsets, not a lecture on Rayleigh scattering. Just a knock on a door, a text, a hand on a shoulder.
Then stand there together, and let the sky do the talking.

how: In many places, people gather at beaches, hilltops and rooftops to watch the sunset together, and some cities have well-known spots where crowds come every clear evening.

p: can any good come from Nazareth?

games.q: you're Philip. your friend doubts anything good could come from Nazareth. what do you say?
o: let me explain why you're wrong.
games.why: Come and see. no persuading, no explaining: an invitation to see for himself.

practice: Let a few people come to mind: someone at home, a neighbor, a friend nearby, or someone far away you could call while you both watch. Pick one, and picture asking them in three words: come and see.
Then picture standing beside them, saying nothing, while the colors change.

wordCard.voice: Nathanael, the skeptical friend whom Philip simply invited to come and see Jesus for himself. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, the words of John 1:46: come and see.

carryVoice: Your line: come and see. In person or on the phone, no speech needed. See you tomorrow.
